HREC-CTX-G2.title: Candidate file: Marisol Achterberg (resume + phone screen scorecard)
HREC-CTX-G2.text:
CANDIDATE FILE - Marisol Achterberg
Req BK-2291, Senior Backend Engineer, Routing Platform
Source: employee referral (Rhys Calloway, Routing Platform)

RESUME SUMMARY
Halvard Payments - Senior Software Engineer, Ledger Platform (Aug 2022 - present)
- Led the migration of the settlement ledger from a nightly batch job to an event-sourced pipeline on Kafka.
- Reduced weekly reconciliation breaks from about 1,400 to under 90.
- Owned the idempotency key service, 38M requests/day.
- "Managed a team of 6 engineers" during the ledger migration.
- Mentored 3 junior engineers through their first on-call rotations.

Cinderpath - Backend Engineer (Jan 2020 - Jul 2022)
- Cinderpath was acquired by Halvard Payments in July 2022; she moved over with the acquisition.
- Built the courier dispatch routing service in Go.
- Cut median dispatch latency from 2.1s to 340ms by replacing a polling loop with a push-based assignment queue.

Orrin Analytics - Software Engineer I (Jun 2016 - Feb 2019)
- Java services for survey data ingestion.
- Shared on-call for the ingestion pipeline.

Gap on resume: Mar 2019 - Dec 2019 (no entry listed)

Education: BS Computer Engineering, Westmarch State University, 2016
Skills listed: Go, Kotlin, Java, Postgres, Kafka, Redis, Terraform, Rust

PHONE SCREEN SCORECARD
Screened Sep 22 by Jonah Pellow (recruiting coordinator), 30 minutes.

Communication: 4/5. Clear and structured, a little long-winded when describing architecture.
Systems depth: 3/5. Stayed high-level on Kafka consumer rebalancing; could not say how partitions were keyed in the ledger pipeline.
Ownership: 4/5. Strong incident story about double-posted transfers and the cleanup afterwards.
Motivation: wants a smaller company and to get closer to routing problems again, which she enjoyed at Cinderpath.

Logistics captured at screen
- Location: lives in Tacoma, WA. OK with hybrid; "prefers two office days, can do three."
- Work authorization: US citizen, no sponsorship needed.
- Compensation expectation: base of $185,000, "flexible for the right equity."
- Notice period: 3 weeks. Earliest start: Nov 3.
- Competing process: in a final round at another company, decision expected by Oct 10.

Flags for the next conversation
1. The 2019 gap has not been discussed yet. Probe neutrally; do not assume a reason.
2. Resume says "managed a team of 6" but at the screen she described herself as "tech lead, no direct reports." Clarify whether she was ever a people manager.
3. Rust is listed under skills, but no role mentions it. Ask where she has used it.
4. Systems depth was the lowest score; the hiring manager should probe Kafka partitioning and ordering guarantees.

Recommendation from screen: advance to hiring manager call with Tomasz.

HREC-CTX-C1.title: HM intake notes: Routing Platform backfill (draft with updates)
HREC-CTX-C1.text:
INTAKE NOTES - Routing Platform backfill (HM sync with Tomasz, draft)
Req BK-2291. Notes taken by the sourcer during the August intake call; updates appended below.

Role and level
Backfill for the senior seat that opened in July. Level: L5 Senior. If the loop comes back mixed we will close at L4 instead; the L4 band tops out at $158k.

Location
Tomasz is happy with fully remote for the right person, anywhere in Pacific or Mountain time. Remote-friendly is fine to say in outreach.

Compensation
Base up to $182k, hard cap, do not go higher in conversations. Equity per the standard L5 grant.

Team
Team of 9 after the reorg, reporting to Tomasz.

Interview loop
Three rounds: HM call, pair coding, past-project deep dive. No system design round this time, Tomasz wants to move faster.

Start date
We need someone by Oct 20. The on-call rotation is thin and the ETA project needs another senior.

What matters most
Kafka and Postgres in production, calm in incidents, can mentor mid-level engineers. Routing background is a bonus, not a requirement. Tomasz does not want someone who only wants to do greenfield work; a lot of the next year is paying down the ETA pipeline and moving the last Python jobs to Go.

Sourcing notes
Target companies with payments, logistics or marketplace backends. Referrals from the team get first review. Two internal referrals are already in the pipeline. Keep outreach short and mention the ETA model work, it gets the best response rate.

UPDATES
Update 9/5: Tomasz wants everyone in Seattle Tue-Thu starting October, no exceptions, including new hires.
Update 9/12: VP said we can stretch to $200k base for someone exceptional. Needs VP sign-off.
Update 9/12: Keep the standard four-session loop; system design stays.
Update 9/19: No rush on start date, January is fine if it is the right person.

Brindlecap Labs | Junior Developer | Cincinnati, OH | Aug 2020 - Jul 2021

Sparrowhawk (open source, maintainer since 2022)

EDUCATION
Ohio Valley Polytechnic University | B.S. Computer Science, Minor in Mathematics | May 2020

SKILLS
Languages: Go, Kotlin, Python, SQL, some TypeScript
Data and messaging: PostgreSQL, Redis, Kafka, AWS SQS
Infrastructure: AWS (ECS, RDS, KMS), Terraform, Docker, GitHub Actions, Datadog

PI-A:JD.title: the job description the user is targeting
PI-A:JD.text:
SENIOR BACKEND ENGINEER, PAYMENTS & LEDGER
Tallowmarket, Inc. | Denver, CO

ABOUT TALLOWMARKET
Tallowmarket is a B2B marketplace where independent restaurants buy directly from regional farms and ranches. Our Payments & Ledger group moves about $1.1B a year through escrowed payouts to more than 6,500 growers. We are a team of 140 people, about 55 of them in engineering. Our backend is Go on PostgreSQL, with Kafka between services and Temporal for long-running payment workflows.

WHAT YOU WILL DO
- Own services in the money path: escrow holds, split payouts to growers, refunds and chargebacks.
- Design and evolve Harrow, our double-entry ledger built on PostgreSQL, as volume grows from 400,000 to a projected 1.5 million ledger entries per day.
- Improve the reliability of the nightly settlement batch that runs at 02:00 Mountain Time and must finish before banks open.
- Lead technical design reviews and mentor mid-level engineers on the team.
- Join the on-call rotation, currently one week in six.
- Partner with Finance and Risk on reconciliation and audit requirements.

WHAT YOU BRING
- 5+ years of professional backend experience in Go, Java or Kotlin.
- Deep PostgreSQL knowledge: indexing, locking, isolation levels, and safe online migrations.
- Experience with event-driven systems (Kafka, Kinesis or similar) and idempotent processing.
- A track record of leading multi-engineer projects from design doc to launch.
- Clear written communication; we make most decisions in design docs.

NICE TO HAVE
- Prior work on a double-entry ledger or a payments platform.
- Experience reducing PCI DSS scope.
- Stripe Connect or Adyen for Platforms integration experience.
- Experience with Temporal or another durable workflow engine.

WORK ARRANGEMENT
Hybrid: in our Denver LoDo office Tuesday through Thursday; Monday and Friday are flexible. Relocation assistance is available for candidates moving to the Denver metro area.

COMPENSATION
Base salary band: $172,000 - $208,000 USD, plus equity and a 6% 401(k) match. This role is leveled at L5 (Senior).

INTERVIEW PROCESS
Recruiter screen (30 minutes), a 60-minute ledger design exercise, a Go coding session, and a values conversation with our Director of Engineering, Imani Castellanos.

Tallowmarket is an equal opportunity employer.

HREC-CTX-G1.title: Brightkeel role brief: Senior Backend Engineer, Routing Platform
HREC-CTX-G1.text:
BRIGHTKEEL FREIGHT SYSTEMS - ROLE BRIEF
Req BK-2291: Senior Backend Engineer, Routing Platform
Prepared by Talent Acquisition for recruiter use. Last updated September 15.

About the company
Brightkeel builds load-matching and routing software for mid-size freight brokers. The core product, Keelway, matches available truck capacity to open loads and plans multi-stop routes. Brightkeel has about 420 employees, raised a Series C in March, and is headquartered in Seattle, with a smaller sales office in Chicago. Engineering is roughly 110 people.

The team
Routing Platform owns the route planning service, the ETA prediction pipeline, and carrier location ingest. The team is 7 engineers (1 staff, 2 senior, 4 mid-level) plus a shared product manager. The hire reports to Engineering Manager Tomasz Evering. Main stack: Go services, Postgres, Kafka and Redis, deployed on AWS with Terraform. A few legacy Python jobs remain and are being retired this year.

On-call is a 1 week in 7 rotation. Engineers receive a $400 stipend per on-call week. Pages outside business hours averaged about two per week last quarter.

Level and compensation
This is an L5 (Senior) role. Base salary band: $168,000 to $196,000. Offers above the midpoint ($182,000) require hiring manager sign-off; offers at the top of the band require VP Engineering approval. Equity is granted as stock options with a 4-year vest and a 1-year cliff. Do not share specific equity numbers before the offer stage; tell candidates equity is discussed at offer. A sign-on bonus is not offered by default; up to $15,000 may be approved by the VP for candidates forfeiting a bonus. 401(k) with a 4% match.

Location and work arrangement
Hybrid. Engineers are in the Seattle office Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday. Fully remote exceptions require VP approval, and none have been granted this year. Relocation assistance of up to $10,000 is available for candidates moving to the Seattle area.

Work authorization
Brightkeel can support H-1B transfers for candidates already in H-1B status. We cannot sponsor new cap-subject H-1B petitions for this req.

Timeline
Target start date is on or before Nov 17. The hiring manager is flexible by about two weeks for a strong candidate; anything later has to be discussed with Tomasz.

Interview process
1. Recruiter screen (30 min)
2. Hiring manager call with Tomasz (45 min)
3. Technical loop, one day, four sessions: system design (60 min), pair coding in Go or a language of the candidate's choice (60 min), past-project deep dive (45 min), values interview (45 min)
Decision within 5 business days of the loop. Candidates hear back from the recruiter, not from interviewers.

Benefits
20 days PTO plus 10 company holidays. 16 weeks paid parental leave for all parents. Medical, dental and vision with 90% of premiums covered for employees. $1,500 annual learning budget.

Growth
Promotion cycles run twice a year, in March and September. The path from L5 is to L6 (Staff); the team's current staff engineer was promoted internally last year.

What we are looking for
Strong backend fundamentals in a distributed system at production scale. Experience with event-driven pipelines (Kafka or similar), Postgres performance work, and owning services in on-call. Nice to have: routing, geospatial, or logistics domain experience. Frontend experience is not required.

Talking points for candidates
Keelway handles about 2.3 million load-match requests per day. In July the team shipped a new ETA model that cut late-arrival prediction error by 31%.

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Why not higher?
conversation: USER (spoken): Tell me about a time you owned something end to end, from the problem all the way to the result.

CANDIDATE: Yeah so, um, we had this reporting dashboard that was slow, and the team kind of decided to rewrite it. I was involved in a lot of the, the backend parts. It went pretty well, I think people liked it.
USER (spoken): What was your specific part?
CANDIDATE: I did some of the queries. And I helped with testing. My lead handled the rollout.
USER (typed to Natively): Rate that ownership answer 1 to 5 and give me one line of reasoning for the scorecard.

NATIVELY: Score it a **2 out of 5**. The candidate describes a team decision and "involved in a lot of the backend parts," but when asked for their specific part they name only some queries and testing, with the lead owning the rollout, so there's no end-to-end ownership or result they can claim.

Ask next: "Walk me through one query you wrote yourself, from the problem you were solving to how you knew it worked. What did you decide, and what happened because of it?"
items.answer:
Because the answer stays at team level: "the team decided," "I was involved," "I helped with testing," and the lead owned the rollout. There's no decision the candidate made alone, no obstacle they hit, and no result they can point to. That's participation, not ownership.

Ask next: "What was the one call on that rewrite that was yours to make? What did you choose, and what changed because of it?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: Is that a problem?
conversation: CANDIDATE (heard): Oh, the gap after Orrin? Yeah, so I left there and mostly helped out at my dad's shop for a while, and I did a bit of freelance on the side.

NATIVELY: That's the gap flagged for this call, and she's just given you the shape of it without any detail. Ask: "What kind of freelance work was that, and what were you building at your dad's shop?" Then follow with what she was doing technically in that stretch, since the resume lists nothing between February 2019 and January 2020.
CANDIDATE (heard): It was small stuff, like a couple of websites for local businesses. Nothing I'd really put on a resume.

NATIVELY: She's downplaying it, so get the specifics before you accept "small stuff." Ask: "Even small sites have decisions in them. What did you build them with, and what was the hardest part of one of them?" Then follow with whether she handled the whole thing herself, from talking to the client to getting it live.
items.answer: Not a problem, but don't let it stay vague. Say: "It's not a problem at all. I'm just trying to understand what you were doing technically in that stretch, so walk me through one of those sites."

items.answer: That's a strong claim to unpack. Ask: "Exactly-once in Kafka only covers the Kafka-to-Kafka path, so what happened at the point where the data left Kafka and hit your downstream systems? How did you make that handoff idempotent?"

items.answer:

items.answer: That's a fair thing to say, and I'd rather you ask it than guess. What I'm looking for is someone who owns the outcome, not just the tasks: who can tell me what they decided, what they traded off, and what they'd do differently. items.question: Before I send this candidate to Tomasz: he wants fully remote from Boise, he'd need an H-1B transfer, and he can't start until mid January. For this req, which of those are dealbreakers, which can be worked around, and what should I say to him right now?
items.answer:
For BK-2291, the H-1B transfer is fine, the brief says Brightkeel supports transfers for candidates already in H-1B status. Remote from Boise is the real problem: hybrid is Tuesday through Thursday in Seattle, and fully remote needs VP approval with none granted this year. Mid-January also misses the target start of November 17, and Tomasz has to weigh that.

What to say to him now: confirm he's in active H-1B status, tell him the role is hybrid in Seattle with relocation support up to $10,000, and ask whether he'd consider relocating or whether remote is firm. Then take the January start to Tomasz before sending him forward.

items.answer: That's a strong story, but the ending is doing a lot of work. Ask: "When you stopped picking up his tickets, what did you say to him directly, and who else knew you'd made that call?"

items.question: So the outage was a retry storm. Our idempotency keys expired after ten minutes, but the upstream bank retried for up to an hour, so we double-posted about eleven hundred transfers. I paged finance within twenty minutes, we froze the payout job, I wrote a reconciliation script that matched on the bank reference, and we reversed everything by end of day. Afterwards I pushed the key TTL to seventy-two hours and added a dedupe check at the ledger write.
items.answer:
That's a strong, specific answer: real numbers, clear ownership, and a fix that addresses the root cause. The one thing worth probing is whether the fix was validated rather than just shipped.

Ask: "After you pushed the TTL to seventy-two hours and added the dedupe check, how did you verify the double-posting couldn't happen again? Did you test it against a retry window longer than the new TTL?"

Score it a **2 out of 5**. The candidate describes a team decision and "involved in a lot of the backend parts," but when asked for their specific part they name only some queries and testing, with the lead owning the rollout, so there's no end-to-end ownership or result they can claim.

Ask next: "Walk me through one query you wrote yourself, from the problem you were solving to how you knew it worked. What did you decide, and what happened because of it?"

items.role: USER: the recruiter / interviewer. OTHER PARTY: the candidate. Natively: helps the recruiter — the next probe, an evaluation of the answer, or the recruiter's own answer when the CANDIDATE asks the recruiter something.
items.question: My biggest weakness? Um, I'd say I'm a perfectionist. I just care too much about getting things right.
conversation: CANDIDATE: Sorry about the background noise, it is pouring here and the gutters are loud.
USER (spoken): No problem at all. Is it always like that this time of year?
CANDIDATE: Pretty much October through March. You get used to it. I just bought a better raincoat.
items.answer: That answer is the classic scripted one, so it tells you almost nothing. Push for a real example: "Can you walk me through a time that perfectionism actually cost you something, and what you did about it?" Then listen for whether they name a concrete instance and a change they made, or just restate the trait.
